copies.headline: Loaded at WR, quietly stole two QBs
copies.body:
The receiver room is the story here. Jaxon Smith-Njigba at 7 overall was value even before he does anything, and Chris Olave in round 3 at WR10 consensus is the kind of pick that makes a bench dangerous. Rome Odunze in round 5 cost more than his rank suggested, but with JSN and Olave anchoring, that's a luxury reach, not a mistake. The RB room is where this draft gets ugly by design or accident — Kenneth Walker at 18 came in above market, Bucky Irving cost a fourth-round reach, and by the time you're trusting Rico Dowdle and Kenny Gainwell as your depth, you're praying for volume more than talent. That's the D grade at running back, and it's earned. Sam LaPorta anchors a thin TE room, with Mark Andrews as pure round-11 gravy.
The real heist is at quarterback: Jayden Daniels in round 7 and Brock Purdy in round 12 are both absurd on cost alone, Purdy his best value of the whole weekend at plus-40. Brian Robinson in round 13 was dead money from the jump. Adam's the reigning champ chasing his second straight, still trailing Isaac 3-5 head-to-head — this roster says he's not worried about anybody else in the room.

copies.headline: Elite top, no floor underneath
copies.body:
Peter built this the way you'd expect from someone chasing a 2022 he can't get back: swing big at the top, worry about the depth chart later. Bijan Robinson at 1.02 is fine value, A.J. Brown falling to him at pick 23 is a legitimate gift, and George Pickens plus Tee Higgins give him three real receiving weapons before Round 5. Then Lamar Jackson lands at pick 50 like a discount code nobody else used, and Dak Prescott in Round 13 is the best value he found all draft, a top-9 quarterback for a pick that usually buys a special-teamer. QB grades out A, WR grades out B+. That's the whole argument for the 2 overall ranking.
Then you hit the RB room and the TE room, both a mess. After Bijan, it's Jonathon Brooks, Jordan Mason, Kyle Monangai, and Chris Rodriguez Jr., four straight swings that all missed, Rodriguez the single worst-value pick anyone made this weekend. Tucker Kraft at TE was a reach too. One injury to Bijan and this offense runs through fumes at running back. Fitting for a Lundquist — brilliant instincts, shaky finish, still trailing brother John 3-6 and still chasing that 2022 ceiling.

copies.headline: Tight End Royalty, Running Back Roulette
copies.body:
John built this thing top-down and it shows. Puka Nacua at #4 anchors the receiving corps, and pairing Brock Bowers with Trey McBride two picks later gives him the only TE room in the league that qualifies as a luxury — an A+ grade there is not a typo. Kyren Williams at #45 was a legitimate coup, +13 on value, and Caleb Williams in round 7 gives him a QB1 who cost nothing. Then the running back room happens. D'Andre Swift is fine, but after that it's Blake Corum, Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Keaton Mitchell, three straight reaches totaling -44 in value, and an F grade at the position that will decide whether this roster actually contends or just looks good on paper.
The bailout: Matthew Stafford in round 13 at +40, his best value of the draft, giving Bowers and McBride an accurate arm behind Caleb Williams insurance. Tyrone Tracy Jr. was his worst pick, -25, dead weight on a bench that didn't need more bodies at a thin position. John leads Peter 6-3 all-time — he'll need the tight ends to carry the backfield's slack if he wants to keep it that way.

copies.headline: RB Cartel, WR Wasteland
copies.body:
The plan here was obvious from pick one: stack backfield touches and figure out the rest later. Cook in round one was pricier than his slot warranted, but pairing him with Achane at #17 for eight picks of surplus value gives Noah a two-headed monster most of the league can't match, and Rhamondre Stevenson in round seven adds a legitimate handcuff-turned-contributor at RB27 cost. Colston Loveland gives the tight end room real upside as a receiving threat, and Drake Maye at #56 might be the single smartest thing on this roster — QB3 production for QB-doesn't-matter pricing. That's an A+ backfield and a B+ QB room built almost entirely off value.
Then there's the wide receiver corps, which is a genuine crime scene. Garrett Wilson was a reach at 32, Mike Evans cost seven spots of value he didn't return at WR27, and Josh Downs and Romeo Doubs both went off the board way ahead of their actual production tier. Michael Wilson at #104 (+25) is the one bright spot, a legitimate steal. Ray Davis in round 14 is dead weight nobody drafts on purpose. Vintage Noah — nobody circles him in August, then he's somehow playing in January.

copies.headline: Loaded Wideout Room, Wobbly Everywhere Else
copies.body:
CeeDee Lamb at 11 is the correct kind of safe, and Christian doubled down with DeVonta Smith at pick 38 and Jameson Williams in round 6, both landing as clear values against consensus cost. Khalil Shakir in round 11 was his best pick of the draft, a WR49 price tag for a Bills target who plays like a top-40 guy, and George Kittle at TE10 cost in round 8 quietly fixes the tight end room too. Then it curdles. Chase Brown and Travis Etienne were paid at or above market in rounds 2 and 3, leaving the backfield thin behind two banged-up-adjacent names, and Deebo Samuel in round 9 is his worst pick — WR56 production bought at a price that assumed the 2021 version showed up. Trevor Lawrence and Jordan Love as the QB plan is the definition of waiting, and it shows in the QB grade.
This is the Aura Farm in miniature — brilliant at the top, chaotic underneath, boom-or-bust before Week 1 even kicks off. Christian's already up 6-4 on Isaac all-time; this roster looks like another 10-4-or-4-10 coin flip.

copies.headline: A Foundation Built, Then Cluttered
copies.body:
Jefferson at 10 is fine, not thrilling — a slight reach given where WR6 typically comes off boards, but he's still the alpha this offense funnels through. What actually makes this roster is the round 2-4 stretch: Saquon Barkley at RB8 prices for value, Jeremiyah Love falling to pick 34 is the best kind of draft-day gift, and Tetairoa McMillan gives the WR room a real complement to Jefferson. Jalen Hurts sliding to round 6 is the headline theft of the whole draft for Logan — a top-six quarterback at QB6 cost, anchoring a room that otherwise grades out C-. TE is a wasteland here, Isaiah Likely a reach for what amounts to a low-end streamer.
The back half gets messy. Xavier Worthy, Michael Pittman, Rashid Shaheed, and especially Mike Washington Jr. at pick 154 all came off the board ahead of their market — that Washington pick alone erases a chunk of the earlier value. Depth at RB behind Barkley and Love is thin and banged-up-adjacent by name recognition alone. This is a solid top-six roster wearing a middling draft-efficiency grade like a bad tie. Fitting, for the guy who's worn the dress and the #1 seed curse both.

copies.headline: Two Elite Positions, Two Empty Rooms
copies.body:
Leif built this thing top-down and stopped caring once he hit the skill-position depth chart. Christian McCaffrey at 1.05 is a small reach at cost but still anchors the room, and Derrick Henry falling to him in round two is real value. Josh Allen at pick 29 is the best kind of QB1 splash, then he doubled down late by grabbing Patrick Mahomes in round 13 — his best value of the draft, a QB2 who'd start for half this league. Kyle Pitts and Marvin Harrison Jr. both came in under market. But the WR room grades out an F for a reason: Davante Adams, Stefon Diggs and Jayden Reed are all aging or unproven, and TE behind Pitts is Greg Dulcich, a reach at pick 188. Round 11's Kaelon Black, RB70 off the board, is his worst pick by a wide margin.
This is peak Joey Lunchbox — stack the studs, forget the middle class, hope volume covers for depth. He's 4-4 against CJ all-time and this roster reads like a coin flip too.

copies.headline: Gibbs Anchors a Roster That Overpaid Everywhere Else
copies.body:
Mitchell's cheat sheet clearly said "get Gibbs, panic later." The Jahmyr Gibbs pick at 1.01 is exactly the value it should be, and Nico Collins in round two is a legit WR9 at a fair price. After that the board turns into a series of bad negotiations — Josh Jacobs at 25 overall, DJ Moore at 49, Courtland Sutton at 73, Rachaad White at 97, all priced well above consensus. The WR room grades D for a reason: Moore, Sutton, Matthew Golden, and Tank Dell (his worst pick, -24) is a lot of names without a real second option behind Collins. Tyler Warren gives the tight end room a floor, and stumbling into Travis Kelce in round ten (+34, his best pick by a mile) and Alvin Kamara in round sixteen were legitimate free rolls, but two lottery tickets don't fix five reaches.
Jaxson Dart and Daniel Jones as your quarterbacks tells you the position was an afterthought, and the D grade there is earned. Mitchell built an RB-A roster around one great pick and then bailed the rest of the draft out with two bench dice rolls. Fitting for a guy who's gone 7-7 three times in four years — even his draft found a way to land dead in the middle.

copies.headline: Loaded receiver room, empty backfield
copies.body:
Chase at three is a gift nobody argues with, and Isaac kept stacking the room after — Nabers in three, McLaurin in four, Metcalf in six, then Wan'Dale Robinson and Jakobi Meyers as cheap volume plays late. That's four or five weeks of stashing lineups so deep you'll bench a WR2 on other rosters. Problem is nobody told him to draft a running back. Javonte Williams at 22 overall was ten picks of reach for a committee back in Dallas, Jaylen Warren cost three slots more than his going rate, and outside of Cam Skattebo — a legitimate value grab in round five — this backfield is a bye-week away from starting a rookie waiver claim. RB grade of F isn't a typo.
The saving grace: Bo Nix in round ten at pick 118 is, by the numbers, the single best value anybody in this league got at any position, and Dalton Kincaid a round later wasn't far behind. Then he torched all of it reaching forty picks early on Adonai Mitchell in round thirteen. Isaac's chasing that 11-3 start from 2022 again — this roster says he's still three years away from finding it.

copies.headline: Jonathan Taylor Anchors a Reach-Heavy Class
copies.body:
Jonathan Taylor at 1.09 is the correct kind of anchor, and Joe Burrow falling to round 6 is his best pick of the draft, a QB4 profile at QB4 price plus twenty-two picks of profit. Alec Pierce and Jake Ferguson padded the value column late, and Chuba Hubbard adds cheap RB depth. But the middle rounds are where this one gets ugly: Rashee Rice at 2.16 and Quinshon Judkins at 3.33 both cost well above their draft slot, and Judkins specifically is his worst pick, a seventeen-pick overpay for a rookie back buried on Cleveland's depth chart. TreVeyon Henderson and Isiah Pacheco stacked more reach money onto a backfield that didn't need the volume.
The result is a WR room graded D and a TE room graded D, propped up by one elite RB and a shockingly good Burrow pull. CJ is stuck below the line more often than not, one winning season in four, and this roster reads like that history: a strong QB idea buried under a backfield he overpaid to build twice. Leif's still tied with him 4-4 — this year won't be the one that tips it.

copies.headline: A Wide Receiver Room With No Support System
copies.body:
Amon-Ra St. Brown at 6 is defensible even at a slight reach, and pairing him with Omarion Hampton's value in round two is a fine start. Then the wheels come off. Zay Flowers nine slots early, Jaylen Waddle, Christian Watson — that's three straight receivers taken well above their going rate, and the room still grades out as this roster's clear strength, which tells you everything about the rest of the build. Running back is a mess of reaches: Jadarian Price, Tony Pollard, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, Tank Bigsby, none of them cheap, none of them a real bellcow behind Hampton. Kyler Murray in round ten is a stretch for a QB17. Dallas Goedert in round eleven is the one shrewd swing on the whole card, forty slots of value at a position that graded D+ anyway.
This is what happens when you fall in love with names and pay retail every round. Grant's the 5-4 chaos king in the Logan rivalry, all variance, no pattern — this draft fits. Wide receiver carries it or nothing does.

copies.headline: A Reach at Every Turn Adds Up
copies.body:
Ashton Jeanty at 12 overall was fine on paper, but the reaches never stopped after that. Drake London, Ladd McConkey and Carnell Tate all cost more than the room valued them, and by the time Jordan Addison and Keenan Allen went in rounds 7 and 12, this was a WR corps built entirely on hope rather than price. The one real bright spot up front is Breece Hall in round 3, a legitimate value next to Jeanty that gives Kaleb a two-back plan that at least makes sense on paper, with RJ Harvey as a lottery ticket behind Denver's committee. Harold Fannin Jr. cost too much in round 6, though Kenyon Sadiq later gave the tight end room some cheap ballast.
The quarterback room is the actual instructive part of this draft: Justin Herbert in round 8 and Jared Goff in round 14 were both steals, proof Kaleb can find value when he's patient. Problem is he wasn't patient anywhere else. This is the 2023 worst-to-first champ now three years into treading water at 8-6, and a draft grade this poor suggests year four of that streak is the good outcome.

intro: Three A's at the top and the draft still felt top-heavy walking out of that cabin — Adam somehow left with the best team despite already owning the best record in league history, which feels unfair on a cellular level, while Peter and John both restocked hard enough to make you forget 2023 ever happened. Running backs went in bunches early and often, and by the time the dust settled half the league had built around two or three backs while the other half punted the position entirely and is going to be very mad about it in Week 6. The middle class is fine — Noah, Christian, Logan all playable — but the bottom five is a genuine disaster, and Kaleb somehow followed up a title with an F, which is either poetic or just sad depending on how much you like Kaleb.
